reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Promises the reader will follow a payout onto a bank network and learn to record it so a late return has a place to land

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Summarises three points: 'paid' means only sent, a failed payout returns days later as a new credit needing a four-state record, and the payee must be checked before sending

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Names two failure patterns the chapter addresses: a returned payout with no open record to attach to, and an unexplained balance line it causes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A studio owner's payout shows 'Paid' for eight days while her bank shows nothing, and both facts are true

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A payout is two processes, provider accounting and bank delivery, and 'paid' reports only the first; failure shows up later as a new credit

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Places the chapter in the running example: Mila's €117.47 leaves Adyen for the studio owner's bank, due 11 March but recorded as arrived only on 25 March

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Lays out the order of the chapter's sections

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: 412 Payouts Marked Paid ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield let studios change bank details unchecked in June 2026 and banks returned 412 payouts worth €386,000

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: 412 Payouts Marked Paid ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The harm came from a record that closed on 'paid', so returned credits had no payout or owner and took 19 days to resolve

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: 412 Payouts Marked Paid ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The incident leaves the new engineering lead three questions that the chapter will answer: what 'paid' asserts, how long a return can come, and what should have stopped the transfers

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Processes, Two Clocks: Why “Paid” Means Sent ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Defines a payout as the provider paying its debt to the merchant from its own balance to an outside bank account

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Processes, Two Clocks: Why “Paid” Means Sent ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The first process is the provider's ledger accounting (received, authorised, booked), finished before any bank is involved

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Processes, Two Clocks: Why “Paid” Means Sent ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The second process is delivery over a payout rail with batches and cut-off times, ending when the receiving bank credits the payee and sets the value date

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Processes, Two Clocks: Why “Paid” Means Sent ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Because a batch rail confirms nothing to the sender, the provider's status after sending describes only its own action, as both providers state

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Processes, Two Clocks: Why “Paid” Means Sent ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The one signal delivery sends back is a return, which arrives as a new transaction days after the payout was marked sent

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Rails a Payout Travels On ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Rails differ by batch versus single processing, operating hours and whether the sender learns the outcome; introduces the table and its sources

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Rails a Payout Travels On ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Cut-off times decide the processing date from the time of day, with current Adyen and Stripe examples that will change

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Rails a Payout Travels On ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Weekends, bank holidays and the receiving bank add further delay, and no provider promises the value date

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Rails a Payout Travels On ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: An instant rail gives a synchronous answer within seconds under EU law, at the cost of amount caps and incomplete bank reach

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Rails a Payout Travels On ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Cross-border payouts add intermediary banks, extra fees and currency conversion, so the payee may receive less

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A standard payout is a scheduled batch of many payments, with the schedule options each provider offers

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe's Payout status 'paid' is documented as able to change to 'failed' afterwards

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe's third-party product, Global Payouts, uses a different object and statuses, where 'posted' corresponds to 'paid' and review can precede sending

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen separates accounting events ending at 'booked' from route-dependent tracking events, and 'booked' is neither final nor departure

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The three provider vocabularies map onto four states an integrator needs, and neither provider has an 'arrived' status on a batch rail

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Both providers book a failed delivery as a separate new transaction crediting the balance days later, leaving the original debit standing

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶7
reverse_outline.summary: Who resends after a return depends on the product: Stripe retries a merchant's scheduled payout, while Global Payouts and Adyen leave it to the sender

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶8
reverse_outline.summary: Neither provider publishes which rail or bank carries a merchant payout per country, or how often payouts are returned

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How a Payout Leaves, and How It Comes Back, at Each Provider ¶9
reverse_outline.summary: A transfer to a valid account owned by someone else never comes back, and there is no general way to undo it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checking the Payee Before the Money Leaves ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Misdirected payouts succeed because transfers are routed by account identifier, not name, so no system on the rail sees an error

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checking the Payee Before the Money Leaves ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: EU verification of payee obliges the sender's provider to check name against account before authorization, as a free warning that cannot block the payer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checking the Payee Before the Money Leaves ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The UK has run the equivalent, Confirmation of Payee, since 2020 as a peer-to-peer API service at large scale

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checking the Payee Before the Money Leaves ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Both providers hand the name-check result to the sender in their third-party payout products, but document no such check for a merchant's standard payout

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Checking the Payee Before the Money Leaves ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The author's rule for acting on the result: stop on no-match, human review on partial match, record who continues, because after a warning the loss is the sender's

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Record a Payout, and What Speed Costs ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The simplest record copies the provider's status and treats 'paid' as final, leaving a return nowhere to go

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Record a Payout, and What Speed Costs ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The second design keeps four states and holds a sent payout open for a return window, whose length is a chosen policy because no source gives an upper bound

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Record a Payout, and What Speed Costs ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The third design buys confirmation of arrival from an instant rail, which both providers sell with a fee and limits

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Record a Payout, and What Speed Costs ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The designs trade cost against speed and certainty of knowing arrival; the author recommends building the second first and offering the third to those who pay

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Ways to Record a Payout, and What Speed Costs ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Paying non-merchants uses a separate product at each provider with its own availability and licensing conditions, and the same record applies

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces a comparison table of the documented facts for the two providers, with the last column flagged as the author's inference

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Recommends a provider-neutral payout intent translated per adapter, storing returns as linked records, and inferring arrival on Stripe

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Payout Record for Two Providers ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Walks Mila's payout through Larkfield's record: 'booked' sets sent on 11 March and a job infers arrived on 25 March after a 10-business-day window, a date about the record, not the money

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Payout Record for Two Providers ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Payout entries pass through a payouts-in-transit clearing account, so anything left in it beyond the window is the list of stranded payouts

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Payout Record for Two Providers ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Replaying June 2026, the new record would have turned the returns into an owned queue on day one / the returns themselves are prevented by a separate name check and hold on changed bank details

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Payout Record for Two Providers ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: For a studio on Stripe the same record is driven by different events, with no arrival signal, and ledger entries come from report lines rather than webhooks

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A timed-out payout request retried with a new key can send the payout twice; a single writer and a key derived from business identity prevent it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A payout can be debited yet not sent because both providers may hold it for review after the accounting step

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: A return arriving after the window closed is handled with a new linked entry that reopens the debt, never by editing the closed payout

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: A misdirected payout gives no signal except the payee's complaint, and provider trace references help locate the transfer but do not recover it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Lists what is established: status reports sending only, failures return as new credits, and transfers run on the account identifier with name checks now required

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Lists what depends on context: the return window's length, whether instant payout is worth its fee, and how strictly to stop on a partial name match

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The author's synthesis: 'arrived' has to be bought, inferred or reported by the payee / controls belong before sending, where the money can still be stopped

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Gives eight questions a team should ask about its payout states, return window, return linking, clearing account, arrival signals, bank-detail changes, match overrides and licensing

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A returned payout is one case of two records disagreeing, and the general remedy, reconciliation, is the next chapter's subject

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.finding: The declared sequence transition (paragraph form) from controls before sending to recording the payout after it is sent is absent; the section opens on the first design with no pick-up of the payee check.
